{{Short description|Average of squared values of a sample}}
In [[mathematics]] and its applications, the '''mean square''' is normally defined as the [[arithmetic mean]] of the [[square (algebra)|squares]] of a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] of numbers or of a [[random variable]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Noise and Noise Rejection |url=https://engineering.purdue.edu/ME365/Textbook/chapter11.pdf |website=engineering.purdue.edu/ME365/Textbook/chapter11 |accessdate=6 January 2020}}</ref> 

It may also be defined as the arithmetic mean of the squares of the ''[[deviation (statistics)|deviations]]'' between a set of numbers and a reference value (e.g., may be a [[mean]] or an [[assumed mean]] of the data),<ref>{{cite web |title=OECD Glossary of Statistical Terms |url=https://stats.oecd.org/glossary/detail.asp?ID=3714 |website=oecd.org |accessdate=6 January 2020}}</ref> in which case it may be known as ''[[mean square deviation]]''.
When the reference value is the assumed [[true value]], the result is known as ''[[mean squared error]]''.

A typical estimate for the [[sample variance]] from a set of sample values <math>x_i</math> uses a divisor of the number of values minus one, ''n-1'', rather than ''n'' as in a simple [[quadratic mean]], and this is still called the "mean square" (e.g. in [[analysis of variance]]):
:<math>s^2=\textstyle\frac{1}{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar{x})^2</math>

The second [[Moment (mathematics)|moment]] of a random variable, <math>E(X^{2})</math> is also called the '''mean square'''.
The [[square root]] of a mean square is known as the [[root mean square]] (RMS or rms), and can be used as an estimate of the [[standard deviation]] of a random variable when the random variable is zero-mean.
